title: Prophet Yahweh summons a UFO for a Las Vegas TV crew

tellings.quote: and a a local TV crew took him up on his challenge. They went to a a local park in in Las Vegas and he said, you know, keep your eyes in the sky. It's going to happen. And all of a sudden, something strange appeared in the sky and they videotaped it and and reported it on the evening news.

discussion.text: Watkins announces in a press release that for 45 days from June 1, 2005 he will call down UFOs for the media over Las Vegas and that a spaceship will descend on his signal and sit in the sky for almost two days.

discussion.by: KTNV Channel 13 Las Vegas (reporter Mike Dello Stritto)
discussion.text: The station's crew meets Watkins at a time and place of their choosing in the last week of May 2005; two objects appear on camera, a white one and then an orange orb, and the footage runs on the evening news. The linked copy is the segment as it circulates today.

A second station tries the same thing days later from the driveway of Watkins' apartment and reports seeing only an airplane: 'We tried, it's a no-show.' The station's own page is gone; the words survive in a forum repost.
Bartholomew lists the explanations skeptics offered within two days (a model aircraft, a balloon, lasers, a concentrated light effect) and notes the site was near Nellis Air Force Base.

Malone says an anonymous site's weather-balloon theory has most likely 'got PY's UFOs pegged' and runs photos captioned as Watkins with weather balloons, adding that Watkins says the man in them is not him.

The reporter is quoted as having gone in expecting to ridicule the claim and come away believing he had seen an unidentified object; the station asked Nellis about aircraft and got no answer. Reported in a 2007 Wikipedia snapshot, the station's own page being gone.

Watkins says the spaceship would never have appeared if he had not been filmed calling it down, blames the Las Vegas media for refusing to film the promised descent, and demands 45 days of standby cameras.

The article offers as one explanation that Watkins signals a friend who releases balloons nearby during his meditation, and in the same breath calls this speculation with no evidence, since the crew chose the location.
Pritchett reports that Watkins' brother confirmed his death from a heart attack in August 2014, and says he is still not sure how Watkins pulled the summoning off.
SharpEye says the first object 'is very much a white balloon'; Duke says they look like balloons and asks whether the station was complicit.
The same poster says the second object gives him trouble: it seems to travel through the clouds and ascend vertically at speed.
Wolf reads the orange orb as a specular reflection of the sun from a distant aircraft, a shapeless blob when the angle is right.
Michels says people have since looked at the footage and said Watkins had an associate who released a balloon, adding that there is no evidence this happened and that it is an alternative hypothesis.
Mishlove answers that alternative hypotheses are often morphing constantly and weaker than 'just the thing happened'.

plain: Jeffrey Mishlove, a researcher with a doctorate who studies the paranormal, tells Jesse Michels's podcast about a man called Prophet Yahweh, who said he could call UFOs into the sky. Mishlove says that around 2005 a local Las Vegas TV crew took up his challenge and met him in a park, where he told them to keep their eyes on the sky. According to Mishlove, something strange then appeared, the crew videotaped it, and it ran on the evening news, which would mean a person could summon such things on demand.
